Mara closed the conference-room door after the acquisition discussion. The announcement was still three days away, but the price of the target company had not moved. She opened the brokerage window on her own workstation, then stopped. Her own account was too obvious. Instead, she called her cousin Eli and asked whether he still had the dormant account they had once used for ordinary index funds.

“Don't put anything in writing,” Mara said. “I will send you a number, and you place the order yourself.”

Eli hesitated. Mara described the trade as a short-term bet on a rumored deal and suggested a small block of call options rather than shares. She told him to split the order over several ordinary-looking transactions and to close it after the announcement. She planned to reimburse him through a consulting invoice so the transfer would have a harmless description. To make the activity look independent, she avoided the office network and used a personal messaging account. She also told him not to mention the meeting, the issuer, or her name.

The plan sounded cautious because every step was framed as reducing a visible connection. That was precisely what made it dangerous. Eli's account had no history of trading options, the expiration date matched the rumored announcement window, and the funds arrived from a source connected to Mara. The broker's surveillance system linked the devices used to log in, while building access records placed Mara at the meeting. A routine review later found that Mara had searched the target's ticker immediately before the conference and that she had discussed an unexplained payment with Eli.

When the announcement finally appeared, the options rose sharply. Eli celebrated the profit; Mara watched the compliance alert arrive. She had believed that using a relative, avoiding workplace systems, and fragmenting orders would create distance. Instead, those choices supplied investigators with a timeline, a beneficiary, and a motive. The scene ends with subpoenas, preserved messages, and the realization that secrecy is not the same thing as plausible deniability.
